clue.text: Seat of - authority, one -for master or dame perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: the Lord Chancellor's cushioned seat in the House of Lords
second meaning: in the nursery rhyme Baa Baa Black Sheep, the three bags of wool are one for the master and one for the dame

explanation.surface: A grand seat of power, apparently allotted to a schoolmaster or a dame.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half quotes the nursery rhyme: 'Yes sir, yes sir, three bags full; one for the master, and one for the dame.' Each bag is a sack of wool.
explanation.definitionFit: The Woolsack is the official chair of the Lord Speaker in the British upper chamber, and literally a bag stuffed with fleece.

clue.text: Gate that may be secured by . catch

definitions.text: that may be secured by . catch

blocks.note: first meaning: a small door or gate, often set in a larger one

blocks.clueFragment: that may be secured by . catch
blocks.note: second meaning: in cricket a bowler takes this when a batsman is caught out

explanation.surface: A garden gate that can be fastened with a latch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secured' and 'catch' suggest a latch on a gate; in cricket a catch is one way of taking a batsman out.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both a small side gate and the dismissal of a batsman in cricket, which a fielder's catch earns.

clue.text: Free 23 of this colour

blocks.note: first meaning: with 23 across in place this reads Free State, and the answer goes before it to name the former South African province
second meaning: the hue between red and yellow

explanation.surface: A free country identified by its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Free State was a Boer republic, later a province of South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a citrus-coloured hue and the first word of the old Boer republic's title.

clue.text: Giving little away in EEC strive to reform it

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Common Market body striving to reform itself while revealing little.
explanation.walkthrough: The EEC was the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU.
explanation.definitionFit: A secretive person keeps information to themselves, revealing hardly anything to others.

clue.text: Integrated college in New Zealand

blocks.note: first meaning: a two-word Oxford college with its name joined up into one word
second meaning: a large city on the South Island, named after that college

explanation.surface: A mixed or merged school somewhere in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Integrated' means the two words of the Oxford college's name joined up, not a school policy.
explanation.definitionFit: The biggest city on the South Island was named after the Oxford college, its name written as a single word.

clue.text: Drinkers in county? Only in fiction

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words
second meaning: Trollope's imaginary English shire, setting of his Chronicles

explanation.surface: Asking whether a county is full of drinkers, and being told that happens only in novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Barsetshire, shortened to Barset, is the fictional county of Anthony Trollope's Barchester novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope invented the shire for his novels, and split apart the word describes the crowd who hang around pubs.

clue.text: Othello, say, wrongly suspected one

blocks.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice, so he is an example of a Moor

explanation.surface: Othello, as an example of a man who wrongly suspected someone.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate sound signal; the clue relies on 'a Moor' and the French word for love being said alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello falsely believed Desdemona was having a love affair with Cassio, and a love affair is called this.

clue.text: One who's not late, being extremely fit?

definitions.text: One who's not late, being extremely fit?

blocks.note: surface reading: a punctual person who arrives on time, perhaps because they are very fit

blocks.clueFragment: One who's not late, being extremely fit?
blocks.note: setter's reading: 'late' means dead, and the fittest are those who outlast the rest, as in Darwin's phrase

explanation.surface: Someone punctual because they are in excellent physical shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like unpunctual but means deceased; 'extremely fit' points to the survival of the fittest.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lives on after danger or hardship is still alive, unlike those described as the late.

clue.text: Composition of agreements between countries — final points switched

indicators.note: things switched trade places, so the letters named swap their order

blocks.note: formal pacts between nations
the last two letters of that word are both compass points, east and south, and they are the ones that trade places

explanation.surface: Writing up international agreements, with the last points exchanged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' are compass points: east and south, the last two letters, change places.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a written work dealing formally with a subject, a scholarly essay or piece of writing.

clue.text: Court in which Galsworthy wrote

blocks.note: first meaning: the Lord Chancellor's division of the English High Court
second meaning: Galsworthy wrote 'In ...', the second novel of The Forsyte Saga

explanation.surface: Wondering which law court the novelist Galsworthy did his writing in.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a historic division of the English High Court and completes the title of a Forsyte Saga novel.

clue.text: Pursue game here

blocks.note: first meaning: to hunt hares with greyhounds
second meaning: a place where a sport is played or a race is run, as at a golf links or racetrack

explanation.surface: A sign telling hunters to chase their quarry at this spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunting hares with greyhounds is called coursing, and a golf links or racetrack is likewise called by this word.

clue.text: Arranging trip into area you first came from'

definitions.text: Arranging trip into area you first came from'

indicators.note: arranging means putting in a new order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Organising a journey back to one's homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and the first part of it also supplies the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Repatriation means sending or bringing someone back to their own country of origin or citizenship.

clue.text: Keen to get a hearing — such a bore!

indicators.note: a hearing is something listened to, so the word that goes before is taken by its sound

blocks.note: keen means enthusiastic, and the synonym is pronounced like the tidal word

explanation.surface: Someone desperate to be listened to, which makes them tiresome company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a dull person; here it is a tidal bore, a wave surging up a river.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagre is the old name for a tidal wave rushing up an estuary, such as the one on the River Severn or Trent.

clue.text: Plant or sort of grass m perfect condition

blocks.note: spear grass is a kind of grass
in mint condition means as good as new

explanation.surface: Describing a plant, or perhaps some grass, that is in flawless shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'm' in the printed clue is a misprint for 'in', which simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearmint is a common garden herb of the mint family, used to flavour chewing gum and sauces.

clue.text: Game little ships do, when it's rough

definitions.text: little ships do, when it's rough

blocks.note: first meaning: a gambling game where coins are thrown towards a mark and then tossed

blocks.clueFragment: little ships do, when it's rough
blocks.note: second meaning: small boats lurch fore and aft and roll about in heavy seas

explanation.surface: Small boats in a game of their own whenever the sea turns rough.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of an old coin-throwing gambling game, and describes the motion of small craft in heavy weather.

clue.text: Trim garment reduced

blocks.note: a frock is a garment
as in prices being down

explanation.surface: A neat item of clothing marked down in price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trim' looks like an adjective for neat; here it is a verb meaning to rebuke.
explanation.definitionFit: To trim someone is an old sense meaning to scold or thrash, just as to dress down is to reprimand severely.

clue.text: Pertinacious advocate has second puzzling question

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
a tickler is a puzzle or tricky problem

explanation.surface: A dogged lawyer comes up with another baffling question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advocate' looks like a barrister; it means a champion of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists stubbornly on something, such as rules or accuracy, championing it persistently.

clue.text: Thoroughfare leading to destruction reported St Matthew

definitions.text: leading to destruction reported St Matthew

blocks.note: first meaning: a wide main road, or New York's theatre street

blocks.clueFragment: leading to destruction reported St Matthew
blocks.note: second meaning: Matthew 7:13 says 'wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction'

explanation.surface: St Matthew warning of a road that ends in ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gospel phrase splits into two words that, joined, are also New York's famous theatre street.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a wide main road, and the Manhattan avenue, as well as the biblical road to perdition.

clue.text: Holmes found one missing Rugby man

blocks.note: first meaning: 'The Adventure of the Missing ...' is a Sherlock Holmes story
second meaning: a player in the back line of a rugby team

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes discovered that a rugby player had gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Conan Doyle story Holmes tracks down a vanished Cambridge rugby player, Godfrey Staunton.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the four backs between the halves and the full-back are called by this title, and Conan Doyle used it in a title.

clue.text: Cook went there for fruit — excellent one

blocks.note: the haw is the berry of the hawthorn
A1 means first-rate, with the 1 written as the letter I
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cook travelled somewhere to buy some fine fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' is Captain James Cook, the explorer, not a chef; he reached these islands in 1778 and was killed there.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Cook landed on these Pacific islands, which he named the Sandwich Islands, and died there in 1779.

clue.text: Provocation from Pravda?

blocks.note: first meaning: something that enrages
second meaning: the Soviet Communist newspaper, a 'red' paper, with rag being slang for a newspaper

explanation.surface: Something inflammatory printed in the Soviet newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Pravda was the official newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party; 'rag' is British slang for a low-grade newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means anything that provokes fury, and also fits a communist newspaper humorously.

clue.text: Repetition of tea dance

blocks.note: cha is slang for tea, here said over and over: three times

explanation.surface: A tea dance where the same tea is served again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea dance' looks like a single phrase, a dance held at teatime; the split comes between tea and dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha-cha is a lively Latin American ballroom dance of Cuban origin, with a triple step.

clue.text: Does he omit nothing for the orchestra?

blocks.note: taken as written
leaving nothing out means including everything

explanation.surface: Asking whether a conductor skips nothing in the score for his orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: The question is cryptic: 'he' omitting nothing means he holds everything inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hallé is the Manchester symphony orchestra founded in 1858 by the pianist Sir Charles Hallé.

clue.text: Rank condition of 19, finally

blocks.note: first meaning: social standing or situation
second meaning: 19 down became the fiftieth and last US member in 1959

explanation.surface: A rank condition, like something gone bad, found at the end of another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like an adjective meaning foul; it is a noun for status. 19 is the Pacific islands that were the last to join the Union.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both status or condition and a constituent member of the USA, which those islands finally became.

clue.text: Look thoroughly for US poet

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
as in 'well done', meaning fully

explanation.surface: Advice to search carefully when hunting for an American poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Lowell, James Russell Lowell and Amy Lowell were all American poets bearing this surname.

clue.text: Youngster carries letter from Greece for monstrous Cretan

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it inside, so the first word wraps round the second

blocks.note: a minor is a person under legal age
the Greek letter equivalent to T

explanation.surface: A child brings home a letter posted from Greece for a Cretan monster.
explanation.definitionFit: The Minotaur was the half-bull beast kept in King Minos's labyrinth on Crete and slain by Theseus.

clue.text: What Donne does with one of his poems

blocks.note: first meaning: the poet's name matches the sound of the word 'one' at its end
second meaning: verses in general are informally called by this plural

explanation.surface: Asking what the poet John Donne did with one of his own poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'with one' as a word pairing: Donne and one share the same sound. Verses are also loosely called by this plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Two words that end in the same sound are said to match this way, and verses in general are informally called this.

clue.text: Interminable names guide mixed up

indicators.note: things mixed up are jumbled out of their order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: n is the abbreviation for name; the plural here supplies a run of them, three being needed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tediously long guidebook full of names, all in a jumble.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue looks corrupted: the anagram needs three Ns beside GUIDE, so 'names' has to stand for several N abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Something interminable seems never to stop, going on without any conclusion.
